summary: A practical guide for administrators who need to protect the computers and networks of a site connected to the Internet. It covers writing security policies, a range of technical security topics, and how to respond when an incident happens. It is informational and replaces RFC 1244.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2196 gives administrators a framework for deciding what to protect and how to respond to security incidents. It covers policy, technical safeguards, and preparation for investigating and recovering from an incident.

sections.title: Risk Assessment and the Basic Approach
sections.content:
The handbook is for system and network administrators and decision makers at sites with computer systems. It is a framework, so each site must make its own decisions, gain agreement, and communicate and implement its policies.

The suggested approach is to identify assets, identify threats, estimate their likelihood, apply cost-effective protections, and review the process continuously. Assets include hardware, software, data, people, documentation, and supplies. The handbook names unauthorized access, disclosure, and denial of service as classic threats.
sections.plainLanguage: Start by listing what the organization needs to protect and what could threaten it. Then choose protections that fit the value of those assets and review them over time.

sections.title: Creating and Maintaining Security Policy
sections.content:
A security policy is a formal statement of rules for people who can access an organization's technology and information. The handbook says a policy must be implementable, enforceable, and clear about the responsibilities of users, administrators, and management.

Policy writers should consider service needs, ease of use, and the cost of security compared with the risk of loss. The handbook identifies privacy, access, accountability, authentication, availability, maintenance, and violation reporting as policy areas. It also says to communicate the policy and review it regularly.
sections.plainLanguage: A security policy tells people which rules apply to the organization's systems and information. It should explain who is responsible and how the rules will be carried out.

sections.title: Services, Network Design, and Firewalls
sections.content:
The handbook recommends a site-wide security plan that guides individual policies. It contrasts a deny-all approach, which turns services off and enables them selectively, with an allow-all approach, which enables services and restricts them as weaknesses are found. The deny-all approach is described as generally more secure but requiring more work.

It recommends examining whether services are needed and separating services with different trust or access needs. A firewall is one mechanism for controlling and monitoring network access, not a complete security solution. Network infrastructure, routing information, and services such as DNS and file transfer also need protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A site should decide which services are needed and limit access according to its policy. A firewall can help control network access, but the handbook treats it as one part of a broader plan.

sections.title: Authentication, Auditing, and Backups
sections.content:
The handbook covers authentication, confidentiality, integrity, authorization, access, and auditing. It warns about reusable passwords sent across networks and discusses one-time passwords and Kerberos. Audit records should include access events and timestamps, but should not include correct or incorrect passwords.

It describes read/write files, write-once media, and printers as audit-record storage choices, each with trade-offs. Backups should be stored off-site, checked periodically, and not assumed to be clean or complete.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites should control who can access systems, record important access changes, and protect those records. Backups need secure storage and regular checks.

sections.title: Preparing for Security Incidents
sections.content:
The handbook recommends planning and testing incident procedures before an incident occurs. A site should identify contacts, define who coordinates the response, decide what information may be shared, and set priorities. Its suggested priorities put human life and safety first, followed by sensitive data, other data, systems, and computing availability.

When a possible incident is identified, the handbook recommends taking a system snapshot and starting a log. Handling includes notification, evidence protection, containment, eradication, recovery, and follow-up. Afterward, the site should review the incident, its plan, and its risk analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Prepare a response plan, assign a coordinator, and practice the steps before a problem occurs. During an incident, confirm what happened, preserve records, limit damage, restore service, and review the response.
